Charging by friction, conduction and induction

Objects become charged when electrons move; the protons stay locked in their nuclei. Rubbing two different materials together drags electrons from the one that holds them loosely onto the one that holds them tightly. Touching a charged conductor to a neutral one lets the extra electrons spread over both, while simply bringing a charged rod near a conductor pushes its electrons to the far side, so earthing that side leaves it with the opposite charge. in the wild

Electricity works like a sushi train.

Every part of this topic is charge doing one of three things. Sitting still, it makes an electric field. Flowing, it is a current carrying energy: voltage is joules per coulomb, current is coulombs per second. Moving, it makes a magnetic field. Same charge, three behaviours.

The belt is off. Every plate waits at the kitchen, ready to be loaded with food.

The belt starts. Each plate is loaded at the kitchen and carries food round to your seat.

Empty plates roll back for more. The food gets eaten; the plates are never used up.

what you leave with

five things, not forty.

  • Only electrons move when solids become charged: a negative object has gained electrons, a positive one has lost them, and the total charge is conserved.
  • Friction: rubbing polythene with wool moves electrons from the wool onto the polythene, so the rod becomes negative and the wool exactly as positive.
  • Conduction: on contact, excess electrons spread over both conductors, so both end with the same sign of charge, and identical spheres share it equally.
  • Induction: a nearby charged rod pushes a conductor’s electrons to its far side; earth it, break the earth, then remove the rod, and it keeps the opposite charge.
  • Lightning: ice collisions separate charge in a storm cloud, its negative base induces positive charge on the ground, and electrons surge down once the air breaks down.
